passage:
Paragraph A
It is a steel box, corrugated on the sides, with doors at one end and cast fittings at each corner. It contains no moving parts and embodies no scientific discovery. Yet economists studying the growth of world trade after 1960 keep arriving at the same unglamorous object, and several have concluded that the shipping container did more to lower the cost of moving goods than any treaty signed in the same period.

Paragraph B
To see why, it helps to picture the port it replaced. Cargo arrived as sacks, crates, barrels and bales, each of a different size, and each had to be carried aboard and stowed by hand. Gangs of dockers worked for days on a single ship, fitting awkward shapes together in the hold like a puzzle. A vessel might spend more time tied to a wharf than at sea, and the labour of loading it could account for as much as half the total cost of the voyage. Breakage was routine, and so was theft: a crate of whisky did not always arrive as a full crate of whisky.

Paragraph C
The idea of simply putting the cargo in a box was not new, and railways had experimented with something similar for decades. What was new, in the mid-1950s, was the insistence that the box should never be opened between the factory and the customer. An American trucking operator named Malcolm McLean bought a shipping line, stripped the decks of an old tanker, and sailed it from Newark to Houston carrying fifty-eight loaded trailer bodies. The cargo had been packed inland and would be unpacked inland. The port had become a place where boxes were lifted, not where goods were handled.

Paragraph D
The first decade was nevertheless slow and quarrelsome. Every operator built boxes to its own dimensions, so a container that fitted one company's ship, crane and chassis fitted nobody else's. The savings depended entirely on the box moving without interruption from lorry to ship to train, and that could not happen until the industry agreed on a single set of measurements, corner fittings and lifting points. The standards that finally emerged in the 1960s were resisted by firms with heavy investments in their own designs, and they mattered more to the outcome than any piece of engineering.

Paragraph E
The effects on ports were severe and uneven. Old harbours had grown up beside city centres, close to the warehouses and the labour that filled and emptied ships; containers needed deep water, wide quays and hectares of flat land for stacking. Cargo drained away from famous waterfronts to sites that had barely existed, and the workforce shrank drastically. A berth that had once occupied hundreds of men could be run by a handful operating cranes. Dock unions fought long battles over the change, and in several countries the settlements they won guaranteed pay for work that had already ceased to exist.

Paragraph F
What followed was less obvious than cheaper freight. When transport is expensive, a factory must sit near its customers or its raw materials; when transport becomes almost free, it can sit wherever labour, land and skill are cheapest, and the pieces of a single product can be made in a dozen countries. The container did not by itself create the long international supply chain, but it removed the friction that had made such a thing uneconomic. Distance stopped being the deciding factor in where things were made.

Paragraph G
The same seamlessness created a problem that has never been solved. A sealed box moving under one document from an inland factory to an inland warehouse is efficient precisely because nobody looks inside it. Customs services inspect only a small fraction, since opening a container costs hours and unstuffing it costs far more. Smugglers understood this early. Every proposal to scan more boxes runs into the same arithmetic: the delay imposed on the honest majority quickly outweighs what is caught.

Paragraph H
The box has changed remarkably little since the standards were fixed. Ships have grown enormous, cranes have been automated, and software now tracks every unit, but the object itself would still fit the fittings of a vessel launched sixty years ago. That is not a failure of imagination. The value was never in the box; it was in the agreement that everyone would use the same one.

(Glossary: stow: to pack cargo into the hold of a ship; chassis: the wheeled frame on which a container is carried by road; berth: the place at a quay where a ship ties up; unstuff: to unload the contents of a container.)
